Divulge

dih-VULJ -- from Latin divulgare ('to publish, make known to the common people'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To divulge is to make known information that was previously private or secret.

The talk-show host tried every trick to get the actress to divulge details about her rumored engagement, but she gave nothing away.

Worked Example

After signing the settlement, both companies were legally forbidden to divulge the exact amount of money involved.

Notice divulge is almost always about information -- a secret, a figure, a plan -- being deliberately shared with someone who wasn't supposed to know it yet.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disclose: To disclose is to make information known formally and completely -- companies disclose their finances, candidates disclose their conflicts of interest, usually because rules require it. To divulge is to let out a secret that was meant to stay private, often just one piece, with a whiff of trouble about it.

confide: To confide is to share something private with one trusted person, expecting them to keep it safe. Divulge points the opposite way: the secret escapes to someone who was never supposed to know it. You confide in your best friend; you refuse to divulge the secret to reporters.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

withhold: to refuse to give or reveal something

suppress: to prevent information from becoming known

Where it sits · how guarded the released information is — reveal → divulge → leak

reveal vs. divulge: Reveal is weaker than divulge: a documentary can reveal any new detail, even a harmless one, while to divulge is to let out something guarded as private or secret.

leak vs. divulge: Leak goes further than divulge: divulging lets out something private, but to leak is to slip truly guarded material -- classified files, sealed reports -- to outsiders without authorization, usually while hiding that you did it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — di-

prefix — di-: apart, in different directions (a form of dis-) (Latin)

root — -vulge

root — -vulge: the common people, the public (Latin (vulgus))

Put it together

Put it together: Divulge combines a form of the prefix dis- with the Latin root vulgus, 'the common people' (the same root behind the word 'vulgar'). To divulge something is, at its root, to spread it out to the general public -- to let ordinary people in on what was once private.

Use the root in a new word: vulgar

Use the root in a new word: vulgar: The professor's lecture explained how a Latin word for 'the common people' eventually gave us the modern word vulgar.

Word Choice

Divulge is almost always paired with a specific piece of information -- a name, a plan, a figure -- being deliberately made known. It usually implies the information was meant to stay private, and that revealing it may cause trouble.
